A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same geometric reduced-order Lagrangian learning framework. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support comparison; v1 Appendices B-F correspond to v2 Appendices C-G.

before.justification: v1 reports original simulation results for 2-DoF and 16-DoF pendulums, a 192-DoF rope and a 600-DoF cloth, including comparisons and ablations in Section 5 and Appendix F.

after.justification: v2 retains these original simulation results and adds L-OpInf comparisons and a full-order versus reduced-order timing experiment in Appendix G.2.3.

M1.justification: The reported GyroAI parameterization changes locally: v1 Appendix B constrains both A_l and B_l to SPD matrices, whereas v2 Appendix C permits any symmetric A_l while retaining SPD B_l. This is a specification correction; the overall architecture, training losses and inference procedure remain unchanged, with no implementation rerun established.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same unactuated and sine-tracking 2-DoF pendulums, coupled 16-DoF pendulum, rope manipulation and cloth-on-sphere scenarios. The added baseline and timing comparisons use existing coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds Lagrangian operator inference, L-OpInf, to the 16-DoF comparison in Table 1 and reports unsuccessful rope experiments with it. This materially extends comparison to a competing reduced-order identification method beyond the retained full-order LNN and AE controls. Appendix G.2.3 also introduces an analytical full-order model as a runtime comparator.

E3.justification: Table 1 and Figures 2 and 11 introduce relative-error evaluation, with Table 1 also adding position and velocity metrics. New experiments specify L-OpInf training on 15,000 samples and matched 3,000-step Euler rollouts for timing. Section 5.2.3 corrects the cloth's 25-step duration from 0.025 to 0.0025 seconds, consistent with the retained simulation timestep; this does not establish rerunning.

E4.justification: New Appendix G.2.3 examines computational speedup of the reduced model against an analytical 16-DoF full-order model, extending v1's LNN runtime analysis. Existing studies of SPD layers, integration horizons, latent dimensions, joint training, AE constraints and energy conservation are retained.

E5.justification: The new timing experiment explicitly reports averaging over 10 runs. Existing trajectory-level standard deviations, quartiles, and two-seed best-model reporting remain unchanged. The added run-count information does not indicate increased repetition of earlier experiments.

E6.justification: Table 1 replaces unnormalized acceleration results with relative errors and adds velocity, position and L-OpInf entries. For example, v2 reports relative position errors of 13.1 for L-OpInf and 0.00939 for ODE-trained RO-LNN. Appendix G.2.3 adds timings of 113.59 seconds for the FOM versus 1.57 seconds for the ROM. These are added or differently measured results, not demonstrated same-setting improvements over v1; other result tables retain their values.

T1.justification: The GyroAI weight-domain correction from SPD to general symmetric A_l revises a formal parameter restriction. Other mathematical constructions and derivations are retained. The new Cholesky discussion supplies conceptual reasoning, without a new theorem or proof.

C1.justification: The Introduction adds a specific comparative claim that the nonlinear approach is more general and expressive than Sharma and Kramer's linear non-intrusive reduction. The original contributions concerning geometric learning, energy preservation, interpretability and data efficiency remain.

C2.justification: New Appendix B attributes Cholesky-based prediction problems to the swelling effect and motivates affine-invariant geometry. Section 5.2 interprets L-OpInf errors and instability as limitations of linear reduction, while Appendix G.2.3 adds an efficiency interpretation. Existing limitations concerning AE reconstruction, latent dimension and numerical instability are retained.

D1.justification: Appendix F.2.2 documents the added L-OpInf implementation in Python/CVXPY, its four-dimensional subspace, identity mass matrix, sample count and reset procedure. Appendix G.2.3 describes symbolic FOM construction and timing on the same local CPU. Existing RO-LNN architectures, hyperparameters and data-generation instructions are largely unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds Sharma and Kramer (2024), Feragen and Fuster (2017), and Lin (2019). The Introduction and Section 4.1 sharpen positioning relative to intrusive MOR and linear non-intrusive identification; Appendix B expands the geometric motivation against Cholesky parameterization.

P1.justification: v2 locally rewrites the Introduction and explanations of MOR, optimization and training. It merges the former autoencoder background subsection into Section 2.2 and adds the Cholesky appendix and runtime subsection. The overall narrative and section sequence remain substantially intact.

P2.justification: Figures 2 and 11 replace coordinate trajectory panels with relative position/velocity error plots. Table 1 expands from three models and one reported quantity to four models and three metrics. Other changes include resizing, scientific-notation formatting and relocation of retained figures and tables.

improvement.justification: The added competing ROM baseline, documented implementation and FOM-versus-ROM timing study make the empirical assessment more informative. Relative-error displays and clearer non-intrusive framing also improve assessability. The gains remain limited: baseline training sample counts differ, and the new explanations attributing errors to swelling and linear subspaces are not experimentally isolated. Overall, v2 strengthens the existing study without substantially expanding its validation.
